clue.text: Knut Hamsun's terminus?

explanation.surface: A wry question about where the Norwegian novelist's line ends.
explanation.definitionFit: Hamsun wrote a novel of that title, and a London railway station of the name is a major terminus.

clue.text: Scour a new edition for operatic tenor

indicators.note: a new edition of a text reworks it, so the letters of the two words before are rearranged

explanation.surface: A request to search a fresh printing for a famous singer.
explanation.definitionFit: Enrico of that surname was the most celebrated Italian opera tenor of the early twentieth century.

clue.text: Be swift in all of it, recommended Kipling

definitions.text: Be swift in all of it, recommended Kipling

parts.words: Be swift in all of it, recommended Kipling
parts.note: Kipling's verse urges the reader to be swift in all of a certain virtue; 'it' stands for the missing word, a dutiful compliance with the law

explanation.surface: Kipling's advice to act promptly in everything.
explanation.definitionFit: The line in Kipling's poem reads 'be swift in all' followed by this word, meaning dutiful compliance.

clue.text: Suffering American model with share of book adornment

parts.note: someone suffering is ill
the Model T was Ford's famous car, so T can stand for model
a ration is an allotted share

explanation.surface: A sick American poses for an artist who gets a portion of a book's decoration.
explanation.definitionFit: A picture printed in a book decorates and explains the text.

clue.text: Dornford Yates was in commerce, really

indicators.note: was in says the name sits inside the run of letters across the next two words

explanation.surface: A claim that the popular novelist once worked in trade.
explanation.walkthrough: Dornford Yates was the pen name of Cecil William Mercer, so the surname is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Dornford Yates was the pseudonym of the novelist whose real surname this is.

clue.text: First Emily Brontë opus all right to provide computer reading

indicators.note: first applies to each of the next three words, taking the opening letter of each

parts.note: OK means all right

explanation.surface: A suggestion that the first novel by Emily Brontë would suit a screen.
explanation.definitionFit: A digital book is read on a computer or tablet rather than on paper.

clue.text: Some of the very rich, tho nicely treated, may be of the underworld

indicators.note: some of says only part of the run of letters in the following words is taken

explanation.surface: The very rich, however well treated, may end up in hell.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek-derived adjective describes gods and spirits dwelling beneath the earth.

clue.text: Howler in Dombey and Son thus worthy of respect

explanation.surface: A remark about a noisy character in Dickens deserving esteem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Howler' looks like a blunder or a noisy person, but it is the Reverend Melchisedech Howler, a ranting preacher in Dickens's Dombey and Son.
explanation.definitionFit: Howler's title is the clerical honorific, and the adjective also means deserving deep respect or veneration.

clue.text: Guide to Dante — and inspiration to Browning

explanation.surface: A figure who led one poet and stirred another.
explanation.definitionFit: The troubadour of that name guides Dante in the Purgatorio, and Robert Browning wrote a long poem titled after him.

clue.text: Count Nikolai in Russian port

explanation.surface: A nobleman found in a Russian harbour town.
explanation.definitionFit: Count Nikolai is a family member in Tolstoy's War and Peace, and the city on the Don is a Russian river port.

clue.text: Red Rum upset is a pushover in Christie's work

indicators.note: upset means the letters of the racehorse's name are knocked into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
a pushover is something easy

explanation.surface: The famous racehorse, beaten, proves a soft touch in an Agatha Christie novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Red Rum was a famous British racehorse, triple winner of the Grand National; 'upset' rearranges its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Agatha Christie published a detective novel of this title in 1939.

clue.text: Silas Kinsman's favourite writers include this novelist

indicators.note: include says the name is contained in the run of letters across the first two words

explanation.surface: A man named Silas Kinsman counts this author among his favourites.
explanation.walkthrough: Marghanita Laski was a British novelist and critic.
explanation.definitionFit: Marghanita Laski wrote fiction such as The Victorian Chaise-Longue.

clue.text: Fur appears on time, nevertheless accompanying a gloomy message from Lowell

indicators.note: appears on says the first piece is placed before the second

parts.note: skunk is the pelt of the animal, sold as fur
an hour is a measure of time

explanation.surface: A fur coat turns up promptly with a sad note from a poet.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Lowell's poem of this name is a dark meditation, hence 'gloomy message'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Robert Lowell poem of this title closes Life Studies on a note of despair.

clue.text: Preliminary matter from new doctor in unit

indicators.note: new says the letters of the following three words are put into a fresh order

explanation.surface: A fresh physician arrives in a hospital ward.
explanation.definitionFit: The opening section of a book, before the main text, prepares the reader.

clue.text: Ballet at end of play

explanation.surface: A dance performed when a game finishes.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Bliss wrote a ballet of this name, and in chess the term marks the winning move that ends the game.

clue.text: Injured by Whisky Galore?

explanation.surface: Someone hurt by a classic comedy about a shipwreck of liquor.
explanation.walkthrough: Whisky Galore is a novel and film about Scottish islanders salvaging whisky; read whimsically, being plied with Scotch leaves one in this state.
explanation.definitionFit: To scotch a snake is to wound it, and the word also jokingly means plied with Scotch.

clue.text: Napoleon III took it on the chin

definitions.text: Napoleon III took it on the chin

parts.words: Napoleon III took it on the chin
parts.note: not suffering a blow: the emperor wore a small pointed tuft of beard below the lower lip, a style named after his title

explanation.surface: The French emperor accepted a setback stoically.
explanation.definitionFit: The pointed chin beard is named for Napoleon III, the emperor who made it fashionable.

clue.text: General describes war on France with remark on ram

indicators.note: on says the remark is put next to and before the ram

parts.note: a comment is a remark
Aries is the ram of the zodiac

explanation.surface: A military leader writes about a French campaign and remarks on a battering ram.
explanation.walkthrough: Julius Caesar's account of his Gallic War, the conquest of what became France, is known by this name.
explanation.definitionFit: Caesar wrote his own accounts of his campaigns in Gaul, known as his commentaries.

clue.text: Give me some row over a native quarter of Mary McCarthy

indicators.note: over in a down clue places the row above the final letter

parts.note: taken as written
a din is a noisy row

explanation.surface: Someone asks for an argument about part of a writer's town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of Mary McCarthy' merely completes the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: In North African cities this is the old Arab district, as distinct from the European area.

clue.text: Minerva contributes to heathen entertainment

indicators.note: contributes to says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: The Roman goddess plays a part in a pagan show.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman goddess of wisdom corresponds to the Greek deity Pallas, protector of Athens.

clue.text: Soul of Japanese poetic wit?

parts.note: brevity is the soul of wit, so the briefest Japanese poems of three short lines are its soul

explanation.surface: A question about the essence of clever Japanese verse.
explanation.definitionFit: These seventeen-syllable Japanese poems embody brevity, which Shakespeare called the soul of wit.

clue.text: West Australian custom (or Eastern?) of eighteenth-century sectarian

parts.note: WA is the abbreviation for Western Australia
a habit is a custom

explanation.surface: A question whether a sectarian follows a practice from Western Australia or from the East.
explanation.definitionFit: A follower of the strict Islamic reform movement founded by Abd al-Wahhab in eighteenth-century Arabia.

clue.text: First man in ruined olden structure, possibly a tomb

indicators.note: in says the opening letter is placed inside the jumbled word
ruined says the letters of olden are wrecked into a new order
first takes the opening letter of the following word

explanation.surface: The earliest human appears in an ancient ruin that may be a grave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ruined' rearranges OLDEN to DOLEN, and 'in' puts M inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A prehistoric megalithic monument of upright stones with a capstone, often a burial chamber.

clue.text: Possibly elite — or even a paragon

explanation.surface: Something that might be select, or even a model of excellence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'elite' and 'paragon' look like praise, but both are old names for type sizes and styles in printing.
explanation.definitionFit: Elite is a typewriter font and paragon an old printers' size, both examples of a design of printed letters.
